from manim import *

class TeachingScene(Scene):
    def setup_layout(self, title_text, lecture_lines):
        # BASE
        self.camera.background_color = "#000000"
        self.title = Text(title_text, font_size=28, color=WHITE).to_edge(UP)
        self.add(self.title)

        # Left-side lecture content (bullets with "-")
        lecture_texts = [Text(line, font_size=22, color=WHITE) for line in lecture_lines]
        self.lecture = VGroup(*lecture_texts).arrange(DOWN, aligned_edge=LEFT).scale(0.8)
        self.lecture.to_edge(LEFT, buff=0.2)
        self.add(self.lecture)

        # Define fine-grained animation grid (4x4 grid on right side)
        self.grid = {}
        rows = ["A", "B", "C", "D", "E", "F"]  # Top to bottom
        cols = ["1", "2", "3", "4", "5", "6"]  # Left to right

        for i, row in enumerate(rows):
            for j, col in enumerate(cols):
                x = 0.5 + j * 1
                y = 2.2 - i * 1
                self.grid[f"{row}{col}"] = np.array([x, y, 0])

    def place_at_grid(self, mobject, grid_pos, scale_factor=1.0):
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(self.grid[grid_pos])
        return mobject

    def place_in_area(self, mobject, top_left, bottom_right, scale_factor=1.0):
        tl_pos = self.grid[top_left]
        br_pos = self.grid[bottom_right]
        
        # Calculate center of the area
        center_x = (tl_pos[0] + br_pos[0]) / 2
        center_y = (tl_pos[1] + br_pos[1]) / 2
        center = np.array([center_x, center_y, 0])
        
        mobject.scale(scale_factor)
        mobject.move_to(center)
        return mobject

            "Yet, nature's forms are rugged and complex.",

        ])
        
        line = Line(start=LEFT, end=RIGHT, color=WHITE)

class Section2Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("The Scaling Law: Prerequisite Knowledge", [
            "Scaling a shape by factor s yields N copies.", 
            "The relationship is N equals s to power D.", 
            "Solving for D gives the log ratio formula."
        ])
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        # Show a line of length 1, scale factor 3.
        # Divide the line into 3 segments.
        # Show the relation: 3^1 segments = 3.
        line = Line(LEFT*1.5, RIGHT*1.5, color=BLUE)
        self.place_at_grid(line, 'B2')
        self.play(Create(line))
        self.lecture[0].set_color(BLUE)
        
        segments = VGroup(*[Line(ORIGIN, RIGHT*1, color=YELLOW) for _ in range(3)]).arrange(RIGHT, buff=0)
        self.place_at_grid(segments, 'C2')
        self.play(Transform(line.copy(), segments))
        
        eq1 = MathTex(r"3^1 = 3", color=YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(eq1, 'D2')
        self.play(Write(eq1))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Show a square of side 1, scale 3.
        # Show the relation: 3^2 segments = 9.
        square = Square(side_length=1.5, color=BLUE)
        self.place_at_grid(square, 'B5')
        self.play(Create(square))
        self.lecture[1].set_color(BLUE)
        
        small_squares = VGroup(*[Square(side_length=0.5, color=YELLOW) for _ in range(9)]).arrange_in_grid(3, 3, buff=0)
        self.place_at_grid(small_squares, 'C5')
        self.play(Transform(square.copy(), small_squares))
        
        eq2 = MathTex(r"3^2 = 9", color=YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(eq2, 'D5')
        self.play(Write(eq2))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        # Solving for D gives the log ratio formula.
        formula = MathTex(r"N = s^D \implies D = \frac{\log(N)}{\log(s)}", color=YELLOW)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, 'E3', scale_factor=1.2)
        self.play(Write(formula))
        self.lecture[2].set_color(YELLOW)
        self.wait(2)

class Section3Scene(TeachingScene):
    def construct(self):
        lecture_lines = [
            "The Koch Snowflake starts from a single segment.",
            "We replace one line with four smaller segments.",
            "Each segment is one-third the original length.",
            "This recursive process occupies more than 1D space.",
            "Fractal dimension D equals log 4 over log 3."
        ]
        self.setup_layout("Calculating the Fractal Dimension: The Koch Snowflake", lecture_lines)
        
        # Animation Elements
        line = Line(start=self.grid["C2"], end=self.grid["C5"], color=GOLD)
        
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[0]), Create(line))
        self.play(self.lecture[0].animate.set_color(GOLD))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        # Representing the 1 to 4 replacement
        new_segments = VGroup(
            Line(self.grid["C2"], self.grid["D3"]),
            Line(self.grid["D3"], self.grid["B3"]),
            Line(self.grid["B3"], self.grid["D4"]),
            Line(self.grid["D4"], self.grid["C5"])
        ).set_color(BLUE)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[1]), FadeOut(line), Create(new_segments))
        self.play(self.lecture[1].animate.set_color(BLUE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 3 ===
        bracket = Brace(new_segments[0], DOWN, color=RED)
        label = Text("1/3", font_size=20, color=RED).next_to(bracket, DOWN, buff=0.1)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[2]), Create(bracket), Write(label))
        self.play(self.lecture[2].animate.set_color(RED))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 4 ===
        # Placeholder for recursion effect
        recursive_visual = VGroup(
            Dot(self.grid["D2"], color=PURPLE),
            Dot(self.grid["D3"], color=PURPLE),
            Dot(self.grid["B3"], color=PURPLE),
            Dot(self.grid["D4"], color=PURPLE),
            Dot(self.grid["D5"], color=PURPLE)
        )
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[3]), FadeIn(recursive_visual))
        self.play(self.lecture[3].animate.set_color(PURPLE))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 5 ===
        formula = MathTex(r"D = \frac{\log(4)}{\log(3)} \approx 1.26", color=WHITE)
        self.place_at_grid(formula, 'E3', scale_factor=1.2)
        
        self.play(FadeIn(self.lecture[4]), Write(formula))
        self.play(self.lecture[4].animate.set_color(WHITE))
        
        self.wait(2)

    def construct(self):
        self.setup_layout("Real-World Applications & Synthesis", [

            "Biological structures leverage this for efficiency.", 
            "Nature optimizes function through high fractal dimensions."
        ])
        
        # Animations
        # === Animation for Lecture Line 1 ===
        cloud = VMobject().set_points_as_corners([
            [10, 10, 0], [20, 0, 0], [40, 0, 0], [50, 10, 0], [60, 5, 0], 
            [70, 10, 0], [65, 20, 0], [75, 30, 0], [65, 40, 0], [55, 35, 0],

        self.place_in_area(cloud, "A1", "C3", scale_factor=0.15)
        self.play(FadeIn(cloud), self.lecture[0].animate.set_color("#808080"))

        # === Animation for Lecture Line 2 ===
        coastline = VGroup(*[Line(start=np.array([i*0.2, np.sin(i)*0.2, 0]), end=np.array([(i+1)*0.2, np.sin(i+1)*0.2, 0]), color="#0000FF") for i in range(20)])

outline.topic: Understanding Fractal Dimension: Beyond Euclidean Geometry
outline.target_audience: University students (STEM majors or curious learners)

sections.title: The Failure of Euclidean Dimensions
sections.content: Introduce the standard dimensions (0D point, 1D line, 2D plane, 3D cube) and demonstrate how they fail to describe complex, 'rough' natural shapes like coastlines or clouds.
sections.example: Compare a smooth circle (2D) to a jagged, self-similar cloud boundary; the cloud has more 'filling' power than a line but less than a plane.

sections.title: The Scaling Law: Prerequisite Knowledge
sections.content: Explain the relationship: if you scale a shape by factor 's', its size increases by 'N = s^D'. Solve for D: D = log(N) / log(s). This is our bridge from integer to fractal dimensions.
sections.example: A 1D line segment doubled (s=2) results in 2 copies (N=2). log(2)/log(2) = 1. A 2D square doubled (s=2) results in 4 copies (N=4). log(4)/log(2) = 2.

sections.title: Calculating the Fractal Dimension: The Koch Snowflake
sections.content: Apply the formula to the Koch Snowflake. Visualize replacing 1 line segment with 4 smaller segments that are each 1/3 the original length. Calculate D = log(4)/log(3) ≈ 1.26.
sections.example: An animated sequence showing a 'Robot Architect' recursively adding triangular 'tentacles' to a line, showing how the length goes to infinity while occupying a space between 1D and 2D.

sections.title: Real-World Applications & Synthesis
sections.content: Connect fractal dimension to surface area efficiency in nature. High fractal dimension implies more surface area packed into limited space, essential for biological function.
sections.example: Visualize a 'Deep Sea Creature' (e.g., a coral reef) using its high fractal dimension to maximize oxygen absorption from water compared to a smooth, flat surface.
